Topics include: The legal and theological debates on music (Musīqā) — the permissibility (ḥalāl) vs. prohibition (ḥarām) of listening to and performing music in Islam (the juristic opinions vary, with some jurists forbidding all music, others allowing certain forms, and the difference between classical and popular music); The music of the Islamic world — the various musical traditions (classical Arabic, Persian, Turkish, Indian, African, and Indonesian) and their development; The use of music in spiritual and devotional contexts — the practice of Samāʿ (listening) in Ṣūfī and mystical traditions (as a means of raising the heart to God, the use of songs of praise, and the spiritual chants); The relationship between music and poetry — the union of the two in the nasheed and the poetic tradition; The music of the ḥarīm (the private spaces of the family) and the public music; The instruments of Islamic music — the oud, the qanun, the ney, the daf, the frame drums, and their historical significance; The concept of maqām — the modal system in Arabic and Turkish music; The modern development of Islamic music (the emergence of contemporary nasheed and devotional music, and the influence of globalization); The works of scholars on music, including the detailed legal opinions (fatāwā) on the permissibility of music; and the role of music in the modern Islamic identity, including its use in youth engagement and activism. Note: This sub-section is often considered a subset of the broader discussion on ethics (akhlāq) and law (fiqh).
sections.name: Fann al-Mūsīqā (Music & Spirituality)
sections.parentSection: Section 8: Al-Adab & al-Funūn (Literature, Poetry & The Arts)

sections.description: Books detailing the moment of death, the questioning in the grave, the punishment/pleasure of the grave (ʿAdhāb/Qinʿ al-Qabr), and the state of the soul between death and resurrection — the beginning of the afterlife journey. Topics include: The moment of death — the stages of death, the agony and the detachment of the soul; The condition of the soul immediately after death (the departure of the angels of death, and the state of the believer vs. the disbeliever); The questioning in the grave (Sūʼal al-Qabr) — the interrogation by the angels Munkar and Nakīr regarding faith, the Prophets, and actions; The punishment of the grave (ʿAdhāb al-Qabr) and the pleasure of the grave (Qinʿ al-Qabr) — the rewards for the righteous and the torment for the sinful (and the debates over whether this is spiritual or physical); The concept of the barzakh — the intermediate state between death and resurrection, where the soul exists in a different dimension and experiences a preliminary judgment; The state of the soul and its relation to the body after death; The intercession (shafāʿah) for the dead — the prayers and requests for forgiveness; The role of righteous deeds (like charity and prayers) in helping the deceased; The books of the great scholars on this topic (Kitāb al-Rūḥ by Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyyah, and the extensive chapters in Biḥār al-anwār); The death of the Prophets and Imams, and the significance of their martyrdom; and the preparation for death (the importance of repentance, self-accounting, and the good death). This sub-section is essential for understanding the Islamic view of the afterlife and the importance of living a righteous life.
sections.name: Al-Mawt wa al-Barzakh (Death & the Grave)
sections.parentSection: Section 9: Ākhir al-Zamān (Eschatology & The End of Times)

sections.description: Books specifically dedicated to the portents and signs that must occur before the Day of Judgment — the detailed prophecies about the end of time. Topics include: The distinction between minor signs (al-ashrāṭ al-ṣughrā) and major signs (al-ashrāṭ al-kubrā); Minor signs — widespread corruption, the loss of knowledge, the increase of ignorance and immorality, the appearance of religious hypocrisy, the abundance of earthquakes, the disappearance of justice, the rise of the irrational and the spread of apostasy, the prevalence of usury (ribā) and the use of interest-bearing transactions, the breakdown of family ties, and the spread of materialism; The specific minor signs reported in the ḥadīth (the signs of the Hour), including the emergence of the Dajjāl (the Antichrist), the descent of Prophet ʿĪsā (Jesus) from the heavens, the appearance of the Beast (Dābbat al-Arḍ), the rising of the sun from the West, the smoke (Dukhān) that will cover the earth, the destruction of the Kaʿbah, and the massive loss of life; The major signs — these include the coming of the Mahdī, the descent of ʿĪsā, the Dajjāl, the Beast, the smoke, the sun from the West, the fire of Yemen, and the earthquake; The sequence and timing of the signs (the chronology of events); The signs as a test and a warning — a call to repentance and preparation; The works of the classical scholars who collected and analyzed the signs (Kitāb al-fitan by Nuʿaym ibn Ḥammād, Aḥwāl al-qiyāmah by al-Qurṭubī, and the extensive sections in Biḥār al-anwār); The modern discussions on the signs of Qiyamah and the contemporary relevance of these prophecies; The relationship between the signs and the coming of the Mahdī; and the preparation for the end of times (the moral and spiritual readiness).
sections.name: Ashraṭ al-Sāʿah (Minor & Major Signs of Qiyamah)

sections.description: Books detailing the actual events of the Day of Judgment itself — the ultimate trial and the final separation of the righteous and the wicked. Topics include: The blowing of the Trumpet (al-Ṣūr) — the first blow that destroys all creation and the second blow that resurrects them; The gathering (al-Ḥashr) — the resurrection of all souls (from the beginning to the end of time), the gathering of all of humanity in the valley of judgment, and the arrangement of the people in ranks; The giving of the books (al-Iʿṭāʾ al-kutub) — the presentation of the deeds (good and bad) in the form of a book, and the joy of the righteous and the terror of the wicked; The weighing of deeds (al-Mīzān) — the scales of justice, the measurement of good and bad deeds, the record of actions, and the precision of justice; The bridge over hellfire (al-Ṣirāṭ) — the path that leads to Paradise, sharper than a sword and finer than a hair, and the passing of the believers, the faltering and the salvation of the faithful; The Intercession (al-Shafāʿah) — the role of the Prophets, the Imams, and the believers in interceding for the people of Paradise and the people of Hell (the Shīʿa doctrine of the intercession of the Imams, particularly Imam ʿAlī and Fāṭimah); The judgment itself — the appearance of God, the consultation of the books, the questioning of the prophets and the communities, and the final separation; The final abode — the entrance into Paradise or the entrance into Hell, the eternal abode, and the vision of God for the righteous; The books on the events of the Day of Judgment (the chapters on Qiyamah in the comprehensive fiqh and ḥadīth works, and the detailed descriptions in the works of al-Ṭūsī and al-Mufīd); The significance of belief in the Day of Judgment for the moral life, and the ethical and theological implications.

sections.description: Books describing the literal and spiritual realities of Heaven and Hell, their levels, the types of people in each, and the eternal nature of the afterlife. Topics include: The description of Paradise (al-Jannah) — the lush gardens, rivers of milk, honey, and wine (non-intoxicating), the palaces, the company of the righteous, the contentment, the eternal joy, and the vision of God; The levels of Paradise (the highest level is the Firdaws, and the lower levels for the believers of different degrees of righteousness), and the ranks of the inhabitants; The description of Hellfire (al-Nār) — the fire, the chains, the torment, the anguish, the regret, and the despair; The levels of Hell (the various depths), the duration of punishment (the difference between eternal punishment for the polytheists and the temporal punishment for the sinful believers), and the hope of salvation; The concept of the vision of God (al-ruʾyah) — the beating vision of God for the believers; The books that describe Paradise and Hell (Ṣifat al-Jannah wa al-Nār by Ibn Abī al-Dunyā, the detailed sections in Biḥār al-anwār, and the commentaries on the Qurʾānic verses describing the afterlife); The theological implications of Paradise and Hell — the doctrine of justice (ʿadl), mercy, and punishment; The ethical function of belief in Paradise and Hell — the motivation for righteousness and the fear of punishment; The discussions on the nature of the afterlife (the physical vs. spiritual debate) and the debates over the duration of punishment; and the significance of these concepts for the spiritual life and for the preparation for the meeting with God.

sections.description: Books dedicated to the figure of Imam al-Mahdī (a.s), the 12th Imam, his birth, his occultations (al-ghaybah al-ṣughrā and al-ghaybah al-kubrā), his role as the savior, and his eschatological mission to fill the earth with justice after it has been filled with tyranny. Topics include: The life of Imam al-Mahdī (a.s) — his birth in Sāmarrā in 255 AH/869 CE, his lineage (the son of Imam al-ʿAskarī a.s), and his status as the 12th and final Imam; The minor occultation (al-ghaybah al-ṣughrā) — the period from his birth until 329 AH/940 CE when he was in contact with his followers through appointed deputies (sufarāʾ), and the nature of the deputies and the questions they addressed; The major occultation (al-ghaybah al-kubrā) — the period from 329 AH/940 CE to the present, where he is alive and awaiting the command of God to emerge; The concept of the return (al-rajʿah) — the unique Shīʿa belief in the return of the dead before Qiyamah, the return of the Imams, and the role of the Mahdī in exacting justice and vengeance on the oppressors; The signs of his reappearance (ʿalāmāt al-ẓuhūr) — the specific events that will precede his emergence (the revolt of the Sufyānī, the uprising of the Yamānī, the call from the heavens, the massacre of the Ashʿarīs, etc.); The global government of the Mahdī — his role as the world leader, the establishment of a global, just government, the filling of the earth with justice and equity, the defeat of oppression, and the conversion of the world to true Islam; The books and traditions about the Mahdī — the major works on al-ghaybah (Al-Ghaybah by al-Nuʿmānī and Al-Ghaybah by Shaykh al-Ṭūsī), the comprehensive work Ikmāl al-dīn by al-Ṣadūq, and the prophecies and traditions on the Mahdī that are found in the comprehensive hadith collections; The concept of the Mahdī in Sunni eschatology (the difference between the Shīʿa and Sunni views — the Sunni belief in a Mahdī figure as a righteous caliph, not a divinely appointed Imam; but many Sunnis also have a tradition of a coming Mahdī); The modern interpretations of the Mahdī and the anticipation of his coming; The role of believers during the occultation — the practical guidance for the believer in the absence of the Imam (the principles of taqlīd and the waiting for the Imam); The contemporary relevance of the doctrine of the Mahdī — the importance of justice, patience, and preparation in the waiting period; and the literature of the Imams concerning the occultation, the emergence, and the final victory.
